Correct Answer: More than 20% Crude Protein and less than 18% Crude Fibre

Protein supplements are defined as feedstuffs containing more than 20% Crude Protein (CP) and less than 18% Crude Fibre (CF). They are distinct from energy feeds (which have CP <20%) and roughage (which has CF >18%).

Feed Classification Summary
Feed TypeCP %CF %Examples

posts.post_content: Streptococcus bovis is a:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Starch-digesting bacteria

Streptococcus bovis is a key starch-digesting bacterium in the rumen. It rapidly ferments starch to lactic acid, and can cause rumen acidosis (grain overload) when starch-rich diets are fed suddenly, as it produces excess lactic acid faster than it can be cleared.

Ruminal Bacteria — Classification
TypeKey Bacteria
Cellulose-digestingFibrobacter succinogenes, Ruminococcus albus, Ruminococcus flavefaciens
Hemicellulose-digestingButyrivibrio fibrisolvens, Bacteroides ruminicola
Starch-digestingStreptococcus bovis, Ruminobacter amylophilus
MethanogenicMethanobacterium ruminantium
Sugar/dextrin utilizingSuccinivibrio dextrinosolvens, Lactobacillus acidophilus
Clinical Note
  • Streptococcus bovis is a facultative anaerobe
  • Sudden switch to high-grain diet → rapid starch → lactic acid production → Lactic acidosis / Grain overload
  • Normal ruminal pH: 6.5–6.8; lactic acidosis drops pH below 5.5
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Cellulose-digesting → Fibrobacter succinogenes and Ruminococcus are the cellulose digesters
  • Hemicellulose digesting → Butyrivibrio fibrisolvens is the key hemicellulose degrader
  • Sugar utilizing → Succinivibrio dextrinosolvens utilises dextrin/sugars; not Streptococcus bovis

posts.post_content: Crop suitable for silage making:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Crop rich in soluble carbohydrate

Crops rich in soluble carbohydrates (sugars) are most suitable for silage making because they support vigorous lactic acid fermentation, which rapidly lowers the pH and produces high-quality silage.

Why Soluble Carbohydrate is Essential for Silage
  • Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) ferment soluble sugars → lactic acid
  • Lactic acid → lowers pH to 3.5–4.2 → inhibits spoilage microorganisms
  • Without sufficient sugars → butyric acid fermentation predominates → poor quality silage
Fermentation Types During Ensiling
TypeConditionQuality
Lactic acid fermentationRich in soluble carbohydratesGood/High quality silage
Butyric acid fermentationRich in protein (poor in carbs)Bad odour; poor quality
Best Crops for Silage
  • Most suitable: Maize, Sorghum (Jowar), Bajra (rich in soluble sugars)
  • Low-sugar crops: use 3–3.5% molasses addition to compensate
  • Grass:Legume ratio for ensiling: 3:1
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Crop rich in protein → leads to butyric acid fermentation → poor quality, bad-smelling silage
  • Crop rich in fat → fat doesn't support lactic acid fermentation; not suitable for ensiling
  • None → incorrect; soluble carbohydrate content is the critical factor for silage quality

posts.post_content: Energy requirement for cattle in India is calculated as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: TDN

In India, the energy requirement for cattle is expressed and calculated using TDN (Total Digestible Nutrients), as specified in Morrison's feeding standard — the most commonly used feeding standard for Indian livestock.

TDN — Key Facts
  • TDN% = DCP% + DCF% + DNFE% + (DEE% × 2.25)
  • Fat is multiplied by 2.25 because it has 2.25× more energy than carbohydrates
  • 1 kg TDN = 4.4 Mcal Digestible Energy
  • 1 kg TDN = 3.6 Mcal Metabolic Energy (DE × 0.82 = ME)
  • 1 kg TDN = 0.86 Starch Equivalent
  • 0.32 kg TDN needed per litre of milk production
Morrison's Feeding Standard (Used in India)
FeatureDetails
Based onDCP, TDN & DM
CountryCommonly used in Indian livestock
Published1915; "Feeds & Feeding" book
Indian adaptationSen & Ray (1964) standard; ICAR standard by Dr. S.K. Ranjhan
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • DCP → measures protein digestibility; not the energy expression unit
  • DM → dry matter basis; used for feed quantity, not energy calculation
  • CP → crude protein; a protein measure, not energy measure

posts.post_content: Prevention of coprophagy in rabbit will leads to:

_aimcq_options.text: Decrease in the ability to digest food

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above

Prevention of coprophagy (caecotrophy) in rabbits leads to all three negative consequences: decreased food digestibility, decreased protein utilisation, and decreased nitrogen retention — because the soft caecal pellets are nutritionally vital.

Coprophagy/Caecotrophy in Rabbits — Key Facts
  • Definition: Ingestion of specially produced soft faecal pellets (caecotropes) produced at night
  • Also known as: Pseudo-rumination
  • Begins in domestic rabbits at 3 weeks of age
  • Hard faeces: produced during the day
  • Soft faeces (caecotropes): produced at night
Consequences of Preventing Coprophagy
ConsequenceMechanism
↓ Digestibility of foodCaecotropes contain microbial enzymes; not recycled
↓ Protein utilisationCaecotropes contain microbial protein (B-vitamins, amino acids)
↓ Nitrogen retentionLess protein absorbed when caecotropes are not consumed
Why Caecotropes Are Nutritionally Important
  • Rich in microbial protein, B-vitamins (especially B12), and volatile fatty acids
  • Allows the rabbit to utilise hindgut fermentation products — similar to ruminant strategy
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Each individual consequence is correct — preventing coprophagy impairs all three simultaneously, making "All the above" the complete answer

posts.post_content: The major cation & anion of extracellular fluid (ECF) are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Na⁺, Cl⁻

The major cation of Extracellular Fluid (ECF) is Na⁺ (Sodium) and the major anion is Cl⁻ (Chloride). ECF includes blood plasma, interstitial fluid, and lymph.

Fluid Compartment Electrolytes
FluidMajor CationMajor Anion
Extracellular Fluid (ECF)Na⁺Cl⁻
Intracellular Fluid (ICF)K⁺PO₄³⁻
Mineral Excretion Routes
  • Na⁺ and K⁺ → excreted mainly via urine
  • Ca and P → excreted mainly via faeces
  • Exception: In carnivores, P is excreted mainly via urine
Clinical Relevance
  • Hyponatraemia (low Na⁺ in ECF) → weakness, confusion, oedema
  • Normal blood Na⁺ in cattle: ~135–150 mEq/L
  • Na⁺ is the primary osmotic force maintaining ECF volume
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • K⁺, PO₄³⁻ → major cation and anion of ICF, not ECF
  • Na⁺, PO₄³⁻ → Na⁺ is correct (ECF cation) but PO₄³⁻ is the ICF anion, not ECF anion
  • None → incorrect; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are well-established ECF electrolytes

posts.post_content: The major cation & anion of intracellular fluid (ICF) are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: K⁺, PO₄³⁻

The major cation of Intracellular Fluid (ICF) is K⁺ (Potassium) and the major anion is PO₄³⁻ (Phosphate). Intracellular fluid is the fluid inside cells, comprising about 60–70% of total body water.

Fluid Compartment Electrolytes — Summary
FluidMajor CationMajor Anion
Extracellular Fluid (ECF)Na⁺Cl⁻
Intracellular Fluid (ICF)K⁺PO₄³⁻
Key Body Water Facts
  • Total body water: 60–70% of animal body
  • ICF makes up ~2/3 of total body water
  • ECF makes up ~1/3 of total body water
  • Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump maintains these gradients: pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per cycle
Phosphorus — Special Role
  • Phosphorus plays an important role in nucleotide formation: ATP, ADP
  • Bone Ca:P ratio = 2:1
  • Normal blood phosphorus in ruminants: 4–8 mg/dl
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Na⁺, Cl⁻ → these are ECF electrolytes, not ICF
  • Na⁺, PO₄³⁻ → Na⁺ is ECF cation; PO₄³⁻ is ICF anion; the pairing is mixed/incorrect
  • None → incorrect; K⁺ and PO₄³⁻ are the established ICF electrolytes

posts.post_content: Which of the following is a wet processing method of grains:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

posts.post_content: In Pearson square method of ration formulation, a major consideration is given to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

  • Involves only two feed ingredients (or two groups)

posts.post_content: If an animal consumes 10 Kg Dry matter and excretes 15 Kg of faeces with 80% moisture, the digestibility coefficient will be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 70%

Using the standard digestibility coefficient formula with the given data: the animal consumed 10 Kg DM and the 15 Kg faeces at 80% moisture contains only 3 Kg of faecal dry matter. Therefore: Digestibility = (10 − 3) / 10 × 100 = 70%.

Step-by-Step Calculation
  • Given: Feed DM intake = 10 Kg; Faeces = 15 Kg; Faeces moisture = 80%
  • Step 1 — Faecal DM: Faecal DM = 15 Kg × (1 − 0.80) = 15 × 0.20 = 3 Kg
  • Step 2 — Digestibility coefficient:
  • DC = (Feed DM intake − Faecal DM) / Feed DM intake × 100
  • DC = (10 − 3) / 10 × 100 = 7/10 × 100 = 70%
Digestibility Coefficient Formula
FormulaDC % = (Nutrient intake − Nutrient in faeces) / Nutrient intake × 100
ImportantAlways convert faeces to DM basis before calculation
NoteFaeces at 80% moisture means only 20% is dry matter
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 20% → would mean 8 Kg excreted as faecal DM; far more than 3 Kg actually excreted
  • 40% → incorrect calculation; digestibility = 40% would mean 6 Kg faecal DM
  • 50% → incorrect; digestibility = 50% would mean 5 Kg faecal DM

posts.post_content: A Bull consumed 10 Kg grass hay with 10% moisture and excreted 4 Kg of dung dry matter. The digestibility coefficient will be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 55.6%

The bull consumed 10 Kg grass hay with 10% moisture, meaning DM intake = 9 Kg. Faecal dry matter excreted = 4 Kg. Therefore: Digestibility = (9 − 4) / 9 × 100 = 55.6%.

Step-by-Step Calculation
  • Given: Hay consumed = 10 Kg; Hay moisture = 10%; Faecal DM = 4 Kg
  • Step 1 — Feed DM intake: Feed DM = 10 Kg × (1 − 0.10) = 10 × 0.90 = 9 Kg
  • Step 2 — Digestibility coefficient:
  • DC = (Feed DM − Faecal DM) / Feed DM × 100
  • DC = (9 − 4) / 9 × 100 = 5/9 × 100 = 55.56% ≈ 55.6%
Key Rule
  • Always convert feed intake to DM basis (subtract moisture from total weight)
  • DC formula: (Intake DM − Faecal DM) / Intake DM × 100
Typical Digestibility Values for Reference
FeedApproximate DC%
Normal straw~46%
Urea-treated straw~70%
Good quality hay55–65%
Concentrate75–85%
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 44.6% → would result if 10 Kg (not 9 Kg DM) was used as the denominator: (10−4)/10×100 = 60% — also not matching; 44.6% requires different values
  • 66.6% → would mean 3 Kg faecal DM (9−3)/9 = 66.6%; but faeces = 4 Kg in the question
  • 10% → far too low; equals the moisture content, not digestibility

posts.post_title: Pigment Causing Brown Color in Silage
posts.post_content: The brown colour of silage is due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Phaeophytin

The brown colour of silage is due to Phaeophytin — formed when the magnesium atom in the centre of the chlorophyll molecule is displaced by hydrogen ions (H⁺) under the acidic conditions of silage fermentation. This converts green chlorophyll to brown phaeophytin.

CompoundColourCondition
ChlorophyllBright greenFresh plant material
PhaeophytinBrown/oliveAcid (H⁺ displaces Mg²⁺) → in silage
ChlorophyllideBright greenEnzyme action (chlorophyllase)

  • Brown colour of Silage → Phaeophytin (chlorophyll + H⁺ under acidic conditions).
  • Both are important distinctions frequently tested in examinations.

  • Chlorophyll → the green pigment in fresh plants; converted TO phaeophytin, not responsible for brown colour.
  • Lactic acid → the preserving acid in silage; it causes the low pH that drives phaeophytin formation but is not itself the brown pigment.
  • Butyric acid → produced in bad-quality silage; responsible for foul odour, not brown colour.

  • Each function — pellet binder, mycotoxin binder, and buffer — is a legitimate and well-documented use of sodium bentonite, so All is the correct answer.

posts.post_content: Rate of gas production in a cow during fermentation is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 30 litres/hour

The rate of gas production in a cow's rumen during peak fermentation is approximately 30 litres per hour. The gas produced is a mixture of CO₂ : CH₄ in the ratio 65 : 35. This gas must be continuously eructated (belched); failure to do so causes bloat (ruminal tympany).

  • 10 litres/hour → below the established physiological rate for adult cattle.

posts.post_title: Absorption Rate of Volatile Fatty Acids
posts.post_content: Rate of VFA absorption across the rumen wall follows the order:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Butyrate > Propionate > Acetate

The rate of VFA absorption across the rumen wall follows the order: Butyrate > Propionate > Acetate. This is because absorption rate is related to the lipid solubility and chain length of the VFA — longer chain and more lipophilic acids (butyrate) diffuse faster across the epithelial membrane.

VFA Absorption Characteristics
VFAChain LengthAbsorption RateRumen Proportion
Butyrate (C4)4 carbonsFastest ✓~10%
Propionate (C3)3 carbonsIntermediate~20%
Acetate (C2)2 carbonsSlowest~65%
Mechanism of VFA Absorption
  • VFAs are absorbed by passive diffusion — no energy expenditure required.
  • Undissociated (protonated) form of VFA diffuses more readily → favoured at lower rumen pH.
  • The rumen papillae provide the large surface area needed for rapid VFA absorption.
  • Butyrate is rapidly converted to β-hydroxybutyrate within the rumen epithelial cells themselves before entering portal blood.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Propionate > Acetate > Butyrate → incorrect order; butyrate, not propionate, is fastest.
  • Acetate > Propionate > Butyrate → completely reversed; acetate (most abundant but smallest) is absorbed most slowly.
  • None → Butyrate > Propionate > Acetate is the established order.

posts.post_content: Maximum level of dietary lipid in ruminant ration without affecting fibre digestion:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 10%

The maximum level of dietary lipid in ruminant rations without impairing fibre digestion is 10% of DM. Above this threshold, long-chain fatty acids coat the surface of fibre particles and rumen microbes, physically blocking microbial attachment and enzymatic fermentation of cellulose.

Dietary Fat Levels in Ruminant Diets
Fat Level (% DM)Effect on Rumen
0–5%Normal rumen function; no adverse effects
5–7%Practical supplemental fat range; some caution needed
Up to 10%Upper safe limit before fibre digestion impaired
>10%Fatty acids coat fibre → reduced cellulolytic bacteria → impaired fibre fermentation
Strategies to Include More Fat
  • Protected/bypass fats (calcium soaps of fatty acids) — bypass rumen without affecting microbes.
  • Saturated fats (tallow, palm oil) are less inhibitory to rumen microbes than unsaturated fats.
  • Whole cottonseeds — the fibrous coat protects the fat from immediate rumen exposure.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 5% → practical recommendation for supplemental fat, but 10% is the maximum without fibre digestion impairment.
  • 15% → exceeds the safe threshold; would significantly impair rumen function.
  • 20% → would cause severe rumen dysfunction, reduced intake, and metabolic problems.

posts.post_content: The absorption of VFA occurs in ruminant by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Passive diffusion

VFA (Volatile Fatty Acids) are absorbed across the rumen wall by passive diffusion — no energy (ATP) is required. The concentration gradient drives movement of undissociated (protonated) VFA molecules from the high-concentration rumen lumen across the lipid bilayer of rumen epithelial cells into portal blood.

Absorption Mechanisms in the GIT
SubstanceAbsorption MechanismSite
VFAs (in ruminants)Passive diffusionRumen wall (papillae)
Glucose (in non-ruminants)Active transport (Na⁺-dependent)Small intestine
Amino acidsActive transportIleum (ruminants); Duodenum/jejunum (non-ruminants)

  • Rumen pH → lower pH → more undissociated VFA → faster passive diffusion.
  • Chain length → Butyrate > Propionate > Acetate (lipid solubility increases with chain length).
  • Surface area → rumen papillae size and density determine absorption capacity.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Active transport → requires ATP and carrier proteins; VFA absorption across rumen wall does not require energy input.
  • Facilitated transport → uses carrier proteins but no ATP; not the established mechanism for ruminal VFA absorption.
  • None → passive diffusion is the correct and well-established mechanism.

posts.post_title: Crude Protein Content of Microbial Protein
posts.post_content: Microbial protein contains about ______% CP:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 65%

The microbial mass (bacteria + protozoa) synthesized in the rumen contains approximately 65% Crude Protein (CP) on a dry matter basis. This microbial protein is the primary protein source for ruminants on adequate energy diets and is of high biological value (~70–85%).

Composition of Rumen Microbial Protein
ParameterValue
CP content of microbial mass~65% DM
Biological Value (BV) of microbial protein~70–85%
Digestibility of microbial protein~70–80%
DCP of microbial protein~50–55%

  • Energy supply → more fermentable energy → more microbial growth → more microbial protein.
  • N:S ratio → must be 10:1 for sulphur-containing amino acid synthesis.
  • Defaunation (removal of protozoa) → increases bacterial protein flow to intestine because protozoa consume bacteria.
  • Microbial protein yield = approximately 130–200 g/kg fermentable organic matter.

  • 40% → too low; typical CP of cereal grains, not microbial biomass.

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lavoisier

Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier (1743–1794) is recognized as the Father of Animal Nutrition. He discovered that animal respiration is fundamentally a process of slow combustion (oxidation), conducted the first calorimetric studies of heat production in animals, and established the law of conservation of matter — foundational principles for understanding energy metabolism in animals.

posts.post_content: Anti nutritional factor present in tapoica/cassava is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Linamarin

Linamarin is the cyanogenic glycoside (anti-nutritional factor) found in Cassava (Tapioca — Manihot esculenta) and linseed. When plant cells are disrupted (chewing, processing), linamarin is hydrolyzed by the enzyme linamarase to release HCN (hydrogen cyanide), which causes potentially fatal cyanide poisoning.

Source PlantCyanogenic GlycosideHCN Released

  • Sodium thiosulphate → converts CN⁻ to thiocyanate (less toxic) → excreted in urine.

  • Dhurrin → cyanogenic glycoside in Sorghum/Jowar; not cassava.

posts.post_content: For optimum use of urea, N:S ratio in diet should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 10:1

For optimum utilization of urea (NPN) in ruminant diets, the Nitrogen : Sulphur (N:S) ratio should be 10:1. Sulphur is essential for the synthesis of sulphur-containing amino acids (methionine, cysteine) by rumen microbes, which rely on NH₃ from urea. Without adequate S, NH₃ cannot be efficiently incorporated into microbial protein.

ParameterRecommended ValueSignificance
N : S ratio in ruminant diet10:1Optimal microbial protein synthesis from NPN
N : S ratio in wool5:1High S content of keratin (wool = 4% S)
Starch : Urea ratio10:1Energy for microbial NH₃ assimilation

  • S-containing vitamins: Thiamine (B₁) and Biotin (B₈).
  • S-containing amino acids: Methionine, Cysteine, Homocysteine, Taurine.
  • S-containing hormones: Insulin, ADH/Vasopressin, Oxytocin.
  • Recommended N:S ratio in ruminant diet = 10:1 for optimal urea utilization.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 15:1 → too high; insufficient sulphur relative to nitrogen → impaired microbial protein synthesis.
  • 20:1 → severely S-deficient; microbial activity would be compromised.
  • None → 10:1 is the textbook standard.

posts.post_content: Legumes are difficult to ensiled (the process of silage making) due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: High buffering capacity

Legumes are difficult to ensile because of their high buffering capacity. Good silage requires rapid acidification (pH drop to <4.5) by lactic acid bacteria. Legumes contain high levels of proteins, amino acids, and organic acids that resist pH change (buffer the rumen) — making it difficult for lactic acid to lower pH quickly enough to preserve the silage.

Soluble sugar contentHigh ✓ (fuel for LAB)Low ✗

  • Add 3–3.5% molasses to supply fermentable sugars for LAB (lactic acid bacteria).
  • Mix with cereals in a 3:1 ratio (grass:legume).
  • Wilting before ensiling to reduce moisture and increase sugar concentration.
  • Use of acid additives (AIV method) to artificially lower pH.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • High Ca & P content → minerals contribute to buffering but are not the primary reason for difficulty.
  • High protein content → proteins do add to buffering capacity but the broader term "high buffering capacity" is the direct cause.
  • None → high buffering capacity is the definitive reason.

posts.post_title: Cause of Feline Central Retinal Degeneration
posts.post_content: Feline central retinal degeneration (FCRD) is a degenerative disease of the retina of a cat, caused by a deficiency of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Taurine

Feline Central Retinal Degeneration (FCRD) is caused by deficiency of Taurine. Cats are obligate carnivores that cannot synthesize adequate taurine from cysteine and methionine (due to very low activity of cysteine sulfinic acid decarboxylase enzyme). Taurine deficiency causes progressive degeneration of the photoreceptor cells in the central retina.

Taurine Deficiency Diseases in Cats
DiseaseSystem AffectedDeficient Nutrient
FCRD (Feline Central Retinal Degeneration)Eye (retina)Taurine
Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM)HeartTaurine
Reproductive failureReproductionTaurine
Why Cats Require Dietary Taurine
  • Cats lack sufficient cysteine sulfinic acid decarboxylase → cannot synthesize taurine from cysteine.
  • Taurine is found only in animal tissues (meat, fish) — not in plant proteins.
  • This is why cats must be fed meat-based diets — vegetarian cat diets cause taurine deficiency.
  • Cat is also unique in requiring Arachidonic acid (EFA) from the diet, as they cannot synthesize it from linoleic acid.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Arachidonic acid → essential fatty acid in cats; deficiency causes skin/coat problems and reproductive issues, not FCRD.
  • Linoleic acid → EFA in pigs and poultry; deficiency causes skin lesions; not FCRD in cats.
  • Glucose-6-phosphate → metabolic intermediate; not a dietary nutrient associated with retinal degeneration.

posts.post_content: Starch: urea ratio in diet should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 10:1

The optimal Starch : Urea ratio in a ruminant diet is 10:1 — meaning 1 kg of starch is required for every 100 g of urea fed. Rapidly fermentable starch provides the energy (carbon skeletons + ATP) that rumen microbes need to efficiently assimilate the NH₃ released from urea hydrolysis into microbial protein.

N : S ratio10:1Microbial amino acid synthesis
Water : Urea (straw treatment)10:1Uniform distribution during UTES

  • Too little starch (high urea) → excess NH₃ accumulates → rumen NH₃ > 80 mg/100 ml → urea toxicity (hyperammonaemia).
  • Too much starch (low urea) → N is limiting for microbial protein synthesis; wasted starch energy.
  • Rumen bacteria unable to use NH₃ effectively if diet CP > 13% or rumen NH₃ > 5–8 mg/100 ml.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 15:1 → too much starch relative to urea; safe but wasteful.
  • 20:1 → excessive starch; not optimal.
  • None → 10:1 is the established standard.

posts.post_title: Cause of Brown Color in Hay
posts.post_content: The brown colour of Hay is mainly due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Maillard-type reaction

The brown colour of hay (especially "mow-burnt hay" or "brown hay") is due to the Maillard-type reaction — a non-enzymatic browning reaction between reducing sugars and free amino groups (especially the ε-amino group of lysine). This occurs when hay is baled at high moisture content, generating heat through microbial fermentation.

ParameterDetail
Reaction typeNon-enzymatic browning (sugar + amino acids)
Most susceptible amino acidLysine (ε-amino group is reactive)

posts.post_title: Amino Acid Susceptible to Maillard Reaction
posts.post_content: An amino acid which is mainly susceptible to Maillard type reaction is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lysine

Lysine is the amino acid most susceptible to the Maillard-type reaction because its ε-amino group (side-chain −NH₂ of the ε-carbon) is highly reactive with reducing sugars. This reaction renders lysine biologically unavailable, even though it is still detected chemically as nitrogen by the Kjeldahl method.

Reactive groupε-amino group (−NH₂ on side chain)Only α-amino group (blocked in peptide bond)

  • It is detected as nitrogen by Kjeldahl (inflates apparent CP) but cannot be hydrolyzed or absorbed.

Approximately 40% of dietary true protein escapes ruminal digestion — this is the UDP (Undegradable Dietary Protein) or RUP (Rumen Undegradable Protein) / Bypass Protein fraction. Protein Equivalent is calculated as the average of Digestible Crude Protein (DCP%) and Digestible True Protein (DTP%): PE = (DCP + DTP) / 2. This ruminant-specific measure accounts for both true protein and NPN (non-protein nitrogen) contributions to the protein supply.

posts.post_content: Which of the following assumption(s) is/are true for the calculation of crude protein?

Correct Answer: Both a & b

Crude Protein calculation by the Kjeldahl method requires two simultaneous assumptions: (a) All food protein contains 16% Nitrogen — hence the conversion factor 100/16 = 6.25, and (b) All Nitrogen in food comes from true protein — ignoring NPN sources. Both assumptions must be accepted for the CP formula: CP = N% × 6.25.

  • Only assumption (a) → incomplete; assumption (b) is equally essential.

The recommended ratio of grass/cereal fodder : legume for silage making is 3:1. Grasses provide the readily fermentable sugars needed by LAB, while legumes contribute protein. Mixing at 3:1 dilutes the high buffering capacity of legumes with the more easily acidified grass component.

Silage Mixture Ratios — Rationale
ComponentContributionProportion
Grass / Cereal fodderSoluble sugars → fuel for LAB → lactic acid3 parts
LegumeProtein, buffering capacity1 part
Why This Ratio is Important
  • Pure legume silage is very difficult to make because high buffering capacity prevents adequate pH drop.
  • The 3:1 ratio ensures sufficient fermentable substrate (from grasses) overwhelms the buffering capacity of legumes.
  • This ratio also produces silage with a balanced nutritive profile (energy from grass + protein from legume).
  • If the mixture is predominantly legume: add 3–3.5% molasses + use AIV acid additives.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 2:1 → too much legume; buffering capacity may still prevent adequate acidification.
  • 4:1 → more grass than needed; silage may be low in protein.
  • 5:1 → excessive grass proportion; nutritive value (protein) will be suboptimal.

posts.post_content: Feed conversion ratios (FCR) of broiler, pig, and cattle are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Broiler = 2, Pig = 3, Cattle = 5

Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) = kg feed consumed / kg live weight gained. The approximate FCR values are: Broiler ≈ 2, Pig ≈ 3, and Cattle ≈ 5. Lower FCR indicates more efficient feed conversion to body weight.

Feed Conversion Ratio by Species
SpeciesApproximate FCREfficiency
Broiler (poultry)~2 (1.8–2.2)Most efficient
Pig~3 (2.5–3.5)Moderately efficient
Cattle (beef)~5 (4.5–7)Least efficient

  • Cattle are ruminants → energy lost as CH₄ (~7% GEi) and heat of fermentation.
  • Larger body size → higher maintenance energy requirement per unit of production.
  • Slower growth rate and older age at slaughter vs broilers.
  • Broilers have been genetically selected for rapid, efficient lean tissue deposition.

  • 2, 3, 2 → cattle cannot match broiler FCR; they are far less efficient.

posts.post_content: DCP content of straw is practically ______ while the TDN is about ______.

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Nil and 40%

Cereal straws are heavily lignified mature crop residues with extremely low nutritive value. DCP (Digestible Crude Protein) of straw is practically Nil (0%) and TDN (Total Digestible Nutrients) is approximately 40%.

Nutritional Composition of Common Roughages
Roughage TypeCP%DCP%TDN%Digestibility%
Normal straw (wheat)3–4%0% (Nil)~40%~46%
Urea-treated straw~8%4–5%~50%~70%

posts.post_content: Precursor of cholesterol is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Acetyl CoA

All carbon atoms in the complex steroid ring structure of cholesterol originate entirely from Acetyl CoA. The biosynthesis occurs primarily in the liver and involves 3 Acetyl CoA → HMG-CoA → Mevalonate → Squalene → Cholesterol.

Cholesterol Biosynthesis Pathway
StepKey Intermediate
3 Acetyl CoA → HMG-CoA (rate-limiting step)
HMG-CoA → Mevalonate (enzyme: HMG-CoA reductase)
Mevalonate → Squalene (30C)
Squalene → Cholesterol (27C steroid ring)
Significance of Cholesterol as a Precursor
  • Cholesterol → Vitamin D (7-dehydrocholesterol → UV light)
  • Cholesterol → All steroid hormones (Testosterone, Estrogen, Progesterone, Cortisol, Aldosterone)
  • Cholesterol → Bile acids (for fat digestion)
  • Statins (cholesterol-lowering drugs) inhibit HMG-CoA reductase.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Glucose → glucose is converted to Acetyl CoA first; the direct precursor is Acetyl CoA, not glucose.
  • Citric acid → intermediate of TCA cycle; not a cholesterol precursor.
  • Tryptophan → amino acid precursor for Niacin and Serotonin; not cholesterol.

posts.post_content: Which of the following is example of a very low bypass protein?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Urea and Casein

Low bypass (high rumen-degradable) proteins are those that are rapidly and almost completely hydrolyzed by rumen microorganisms. Urea (100% degradable — no protein structure, just NPN) and Casein (milk protein — highly soluble, ~90–95% degraded in rumen) are the classic examples.

Bypass Protein Spectrum
FeedRumen DegradabilityClassification
Urea100%Completely degradable (NPN)
Casein~90–95%Very low bypass
Soybean meal~65–70%Moderate bypass
Maize (Zein protein)~40–50%Higher bypass
Feather meal~20–30%High natural bypass

Why Low Bypass is Important
  • Highly degradable proteins provide NH₃ for microbial protein synthesis in the rumen.
  • But if NH₃ production exceeds microbial utilization → wasted N and potential toxicity.
  • High-producing cows need bypass protein to meet their post-ruminal amino acid requirements.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Maize, feather meal, blood meal → these are HIGH bypass proteins, not low bypass.
  • Soybean meal → moderate bypass (~30–35%); not as low as urea/casein.
  • None → Urea and Casein are the definitive examples of low/no bypass protein.

Ad libitum (Latin: "at one's pleasure") feeding means the animal has continuous, unrestricted access to feed at all times. It is the standard feeding regime used for broilers, growing pigs, and in many research trials to determine voluntary feed intake.

Types of Feeding Regimes in Animal Production

Molasses serves a dual role in animal feed: (1) as an energy-rich concentrate (high in fermentable sugars — sucrose), and (2) as a pellet binder in feed manufacturing. Its sticky, viscous nature helps hold pellets together during pelleting.

  • Used in urea-molasses blocks (UMB) as a slow-release NPN vehicle for ruminants.

posts.post_content: NPN feed-ingredient is added to ruminant diet at what % of concentrate mixture?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 3%

The safe maximum inclusion level of NPN (Non-Protein Nitrogen) — primarily urea — in ruminant concentrate mixture is 3%. Exceeding this threshold risks ammonia toxicity when rumen NH₃ concentration surpasses 80 mg/100 ml.

NPN/Urea Inclusion Guidelines in Ruminant Rations
Feed TypeUrea Inclusion Level
Dry roughage (straw)4% of straw dry weight
Succulent roughage (silage)0.5% of wet material
Concentrate mixtureUp to 3% of total concentrate
Total ration (DM basis)Up to 1% of total DM
Urea Toxicity — Key Facts
  • Urea toxicity occurs when rumen NH₃ > 80 mg/100 ml or blood NH₃ > 1 mg/100 ml.
  • Treatment: 20–40 litres cold water drench OR 4–5 litres 10% acetic acid.
  • Urea must NEVER be fed to young calves (<6 months) or monogastric animals.
  • Nitrogen content of pure urea = 46.6%.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 1% → this is the inclusion level in the total DM of the ration, not in concentrate alone.
  • 5% → exceeds safe limits; risks acute urea/ammonia toxicity.
  • 4% → used for straw treatment (100 kg straw + 40 L water + 4 kg urea), not concentrate.

posts.post_content: Cerebro-cortical necrosis (or polio-encephalo-malacia) in cattle is caused by deficiency of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thiamine (Vitamin B₁)

Polioencephalomalacia (PEM) — also called Cerebrocortical Necrosis (CCN) — in cattle and sheep is caused by Thiamine (Vitamin B₁) deficiency. Thiamine is essential for pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase — enzymes critical for brain energy metabolism.

Vitamin B₁ Deficiency Diseases by Species
SpeciesDiseaseSigns
Cattle/Sheep (ruminants)PEM / Cerebrocortical Necrosis (CCN)Blindness, circling, convulsions, opisthotonus
Birds (poultry)Polyneuritis"Star-gazer" position — head drawn backward
FishChastek paralysisDue to thiaminase in raw fish
Cause of PEM in Ruminants
  • High grain diets → excess Thiaminase-producing bacteria in rumen → Thiamine destruction.
  • Sulphur toxicity → also produces PEM by inhibiting Thiamine function.
  • Treatment: Thiamine injection (IV/IM) at 10 mg/kg body weight.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Riboflavin (B₂) → causes "Curled toe paralysis" in chickens; not PEM in cattle.
  • Vitamin C → deficiency causes Scurvy; not a ruminant brain disease.
  • Vitamin A → deficiency causes "Nutritional roup" in poultry and night blindness in cattle; not PEM.

posts.post_title: Limiting Amino Acids in Grains and Pulses
posts.post_content: Limiting amino acid (or) deficient amino acid in pulses & cereal grains are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Methionine (pulses) and Lysine (cereal grains)

Pulses (legumes) are deficient in Methionine (sulphur-containing amino acid), while cereal grains are deficient in Lysine. This complementarity is the basis of combining cereals with legumes in diet formulation for improved protein quality.

Limiting Amino Acids by Feed Category
Feed TypeFirst Limiting AANotes
Cereal grains (maize, wheat, rice)LysineCereal proteins (prolamins) are Lys-poor
Pulses / Legumes (soybean, groundnut)MethionineRich in Lys but low in Met
Fish mealGenerally completeGood balance of all EAAs
Complementarity Principle
  • Cereal (rich in Met, low in Lys) + Legume (rich in Lys, low in Met) = complementary protein.
  • Classic example: Rice + Lentils (dal-chawal) — nutritionally complete protein combination.
  • This principle is widely used in human and livestock diet formulation globally.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Leucine & methionine → Leucine is not a major limiting amino acid in standard feeds.
  • Lysine & methionine → reverses the assignment; Lysine is limiting in grains, not pulses.

posts.post_content: Glucose is used for the formation of which vitamin?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C)

Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) is synthesized in the body from Hexose sugar (Glucose) via the glucuronic acid pathway. Most animals (except primates, guinea pigs, and some fish) can synthesize their own Vitamin C from glucose.

VitaminPrecursor / Synthesis Source

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

posts.post_title: Effects of High Fat Diets in Ruminants
posts.post_content: If lipid content in the ruminant diet increases above 10% then:

_aimcq_options.text: Activity of rumen microbes are reduced
The fermentation of fiber retarded because fatty acids are absorbed on their surface

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fermentation of fibre is retarded because fatty acids coat microbial surfaces

When lipid content in ruminant diets exceeds 10% of DM, excess fatty acids adsorb onto the surface of fibre particles and ruminal microbes, physically blocking microbial attachment and enzymatic digestion. This inhibits cellulolytic bacteria and reduces fibre fermentation.

Effects of High Fat on Rumen Function
EffectMechanism
Reduced fibre fermentationFatty acids coat fibre surface → block microbial access
Reduced cellulolytic bacteriaLong-chain fatty acids are directly toxic to gram+ bacteria
Lower acetate:propionate ratioShift in VFA profile → lower milk fat %
Reduced feed intakeSecondary effect at very high fat levels
Practical Recommendations
  • Ruminant diets should generally not exceed 5–7% supplemental fat (total fat ≤ 10% DM).
  • Protected (bypass) fats (e.g., calcium soaps of fatty acids) minimize rumen disruption.
  • Unsaturated fatty acids are more inhibitory to rumen microbes than saturated ones.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Activity of rumen microbes reduced → partially true but the primary mechanism is physical blockage of fibre, not general microbial suppression.
  • Feed intake falls → secondary, indirect effect; not the primary/direct consequence described.
  • None → option 2 is correct.

posts.post_content: Metabolic faecal nitrogen (MFN) depends upon:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dry Matter Intake (DMI)

Metabolic Faecal Nitrogen (MFN) represents the endogenous nitrogen losses in faeces that are independent of dietary protein — they come from intestinal cell debris, digestive enzymes, and mucus. MFN is directly proportional to Dry Matter Intake (DMI), not dietary protein content.

While classic Lactation Tetany (Grass Tetany) in cows and sheep is caused by Magnesium (Mg) deficiency, in mares (female horses) it is caused by Calcium (Ca) deficiency. This is an important species-specific exception.

posts.post_content: Major cation & anion in extra-cellular fluid (ECF) are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Na⁺, Cl⁻

The major cation in Extra-Cellular Fluid (ECF) is Na⁺ (Sodium) and the major anion is Cl⁻ (Chloride). ECF includes blood plasma, interstitial fluid, and lymph. This ionic composition is critical for maintaining osmotic balance and nerve conduction.

Fluid Compartment Ion Composition
Fluid CompartmentMajor CationMajor Anion
Extra-Cellular Fluid (ECF)Na⁺Cl⁻
Intra-Cellular Fluid (ICF)K⁺PO₄³⁻
Clinical Relevance
  • Hyponatraemia (low ECF Na⁺) leads to oedema, weakness, and neurological signs.
  • Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump actively maintains this electrochemical gradient across cell membranes.
  • Dietary NaCl (common salt) directly replenishes ECF Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • K⁺, PO₄³⁻ → these are the ICF ions, not ECF.
  • Na⁺, PO₄³⁻ → Na⁺ is correct for ECF cation, but the anion is Cl⁻, not PO₄³⁻.
  • None → incorrect; ECF has well-defined major ions.

It consists of abraded intestinal mucosa, spent digestive enzymes & rumen bacterial nitrogen

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Each individual statement is correct, making Both are correct the right choice.
  • None → incorrect, as both statements are scientifically accurate.

posts.post_content: Storage form of iron in liver, spleen and kidney is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both Hemosiderin and Ferritin

Iron is stored in the liver, spleen, and kidney in two forms: Ferritin (soluble, primary short-term storage form) and Hemosiderin (insoluble, iron-protein complex representing long-term/overload storage). Both are found in the reticuloendothelial system.

Iron Forms in the Body
FormLocationFunction
FerritinLiver, spleen, bone marrowPrimary storage; soluble; rapidly mobilized
HemosiderinLiver, spleen, kidneyLong-term/overflow storage; insoluble
TransferrinBlood serumTransport protein for Fe in blood
HaemoglobinRed blood cellsOxygen transport (contains 60–70% of body Fe)
Iron Toxicity — Siderosis
  • Siderosis = excessive iron deposition as hemosiderin in liver, spleen, kidney.
  • Occurs with chronic iron overload (excessive supplementation or haemolytic diseases).
  • Prevention of piglet anaemia: IM iron dextran injection on 4th and 14th day after birth.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Hemosiderin alone → incomplete; ferritin is the primary storage form.
  • Ferritin alone → incomplete; hemosiderin co-exists, especially in iron overload.
  • Transferrin → transport protein in blood serum; NOT a storage form.

posts.post_content: Major cation & anion in Intra-cellular fluid (ICF) are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: K⁺, PO₄³⁻

The major cation in Intra-Cellular Fluid (ICF) is K⁺ (Potassium) and the major anion is PO₄³⁻ (Phosphate). ICF accounts for about two-thirds of total body water and is the site of most metabolic reactions.

Comparison of Fluid Compartments
ParameterECFICF
Major cationNa⁺K⁺

  • K⁺ is actively pumped into cells by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, maintaining higher intracellular concentration.
  • Phosphate is critical for ATP synthesis, nucleic acids, and phospholipid membranes — hence its high concentration inside cells.
  • Dietary potassium deficiency leads to hypokalaemia — muscle weakness, cardiac arrhythmias.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Na⁺, Cl⁻ → these are the ECF ions.
  • Na⁺, PO₄³⁻ → Na⁺ is extracellular; PO₄³⁻ is intracellular — mixed pair.

posts.post_content: Chromic oxide is commonly used marker in digestion trial of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above (Avian, Swine, Carnivores)

Chromic oxide (Cr₂O₃) is a completely indigestible, non-absorbed external marker used in digestibility trials across multiple species including avian, swine, and carnivores. It is given in known quantities and the ratio of marker to nutrient in faeces gives apparent digestibility.

SpeciesChromic Oxide Used?Notes
Avian (poultry)Yes ✓Useful because of cloaca collection challenge
Swine (pig)Yes ✓Common in digestibility research

  • Known amount of indigestible marker → consumed with feed.
  • Ratio of marker concentration in feed vs faeces → digestibility coefficient.
  • Internal indicators: Lignin, Silica, Acid Insoluble Ash (AIA).
  • External indicators: Chromic oxide, Ferric oxide, Chromium-EDTA, Cerium.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Selecting only one species (Avian, Swine, or Carnivores alone) is incomplete — chromic oxide is used in all three.

posts.post_content: Iron transport protein in blood is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Transferrin

Transferrin (also called siderophilin) is the specific iron transport protein in blood serum. It carries iron (Fe³⁺) from storage sites (liver) and absorption sites (intestinal mucosa) to utilization sites (bone marrow for haemoglobin synthesis).

Iron Metabolism Proteins
ProteinLocationRole
TransferrinBlood serumFe³⁺ transport → bone marrow, tissues
FerritinLiver, spleen, bone marrow cellsShort-term iron STORAGE
HemosiderinLiver, spleen, kidney cellsLong-term iron STORAGE (overflow)

  • Serum transferrin saturation (%) is used to assess iron status: normal = 20–50%.
  • In iron deficiency anaemia → transferrin is high (more binding capacity unused) but saturation is low.
  • In iron overload (haemochromatosis/siderosis) → transferrin is low and nearly fully saturated.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Hemosiderin → intracellular storage form; not a blood transport protein.
  • Ferritin → intracellular storage protein; serum ferritin levels exist but it is not the transport form.
  • All the above → only Transferrin is the transport protein in serum.

posts.post_title: Excretion Pathways for Sodium and Potassium
posts.post_content: Main path of excretion of Ca & P is faeces, while the main path of excretion of $Na^{+}$ & $K^{+}$ is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Urine

While Ca and P are primarily excreted via faeces, the mineral ions Na⁺ and K⁺ are primarily excreted via urine. This difference reflects the renal regulation of monovalent ions and the intestinal/biliary secretion pathway for divalent minerals.

Excretion Pathways of Key Minerals
MineralPrimary Excretion RouteException
Ca, PFaecesIn carnivores, P → urine
Na⁺, K⁺Urine—
MgFaeces + Urine—
Hormonal Regulation
  • Aldosterone (adrenal cortex) regulates Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ excretion in renal tubules.
  • The kidneys are the primary site of Na⁺/K⁺ homeostasis.
  • Sweat contains Na⁺ and K⁺ but is not the primary excretory route.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Faeces → the route for Ca and P, not Na⁺/K⁺.
  • Sweat → a minor route; not the primary excretion pathway.
  • None → urine IS the correct answer.

posts.post_title: Limitations of Chromic Oxide in Digestion Trials
posts.post_content: Chromic oxide is not commonly used in ______ because it does not give accurate results:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Herbivores

Chromic oxide is avoided in herbivores (ruminants) because it does not pass through the rumen at a uniform rate — it segregates with different particle sizes and densities, giving inaccurate digestibility estimates. Internal markers like Acid Insoluble Ash (AIA) or lignin are preferred for ruminants.

Digestibility Markers — Comparison
Marker TypeExamplesBest Suited For
External — accurate in non-ruminantsChromic oxide (Cr₂O₃), Ferric oxideSwine, poultry, carnivores
Internal — preferred for ruminantsAIA, Lignin, SilicaRuminants (cattle, sheep, goat)
Radioisotope markersCr-EDTA, ⁵¹Cr, CeriumLiquid vs solid phase in ruminants
Why Chromic Oxide Fails in Ruminants
  • Rumen has differential passage rates for fine vs coarse particles — chromic oxide settles with heavy particles, overestimating faecal output of some fractions.
  • Results in overestimation of digestibility in some periods and underestimation in others.
  • AIA (endogenous silicates in feed) is a more reliable internal marker for ruminants.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Carnivores → chromic oxide works well in carnivores; no segregation issue in simple stomachs.
  • Birds → used in poultry; though cloaca presents challenges, chromic oxide itself is accurate.
  • None → herbivores IS the correct exclusion group.

posts.post_content: Pernicious anemia is caused due to deficiency of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vitamin B₁₂ (Cyanocobalamin)

Pernicious anaemia is a specific type of megaloblastic anaemia caused by Vitamin B₁₂ (Cyanocobalamin) deficiency. It occurs when the stomach fails to produce Intrinsic Factor — the glycoprotein required for B₁₂ absorption in the ileum.

Vitamin B₁₂ — Key Facts
ParameterDetail
Chemical nameCyanocobalamin
Other namesAnti-pernicious anaemia factor; Animal protein factor; Chick growth factor
Mineral containedCobalt (Co) — only vitamin with a mineral in its structure
Absorption siteIleum (requires Intrinsic Factor from stomach)
SynthesisBy rumen microbes in ruminants
Anaemia Types — Differential Diagnosis
  • Pernicious anaemia → B₁₂ deficiency → megaloblastic anaemia (large immature RBCs).
  • Iron deficiency anaemia → microcytic hypochromic anaemia.
  • Folic acid deficiency → megaloblastic anaemia (similar to B₁₂ — both needed for DNA synthesis).
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Iron → deficiency causes iron deficiency anaemia (microcytic), not pernicious anaemia.
  • Folic acid → also causes megaloblastic anaemia, but pernicious anaemia is specifically B₁₂-mediated.
  • All → only B₁₂ is directly associated with the classic "pernicious anaemia" diagnosis.

posts.post_content: Main route of phosphorus excretion in carnivores is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Urine

In carnivores, the primary route of phosphorus excretion is via urine, unlike herbivores and ruminants where faeces is the main route. This is because carnivores have a high protein/phosphorus diet and their kidneys efficiently filter and excrete inorganic phosphate.

Phosphorus Excretion by Species
Species TypePrimary P Excretion Route
Herbivores/RuminantsFaeces (via bile & intestinal secretion)
Carnivores (dog, cat)Urine
Omnivores (pig, human)Faeces (primarily)
Why This Difference Exists
  • Carnivore diets are rich in animal protein → high phosphorus intake → excreted renally.
  • Ruminants recycle P heavily through saliva and re-absorb it in the intestine → mainly faecal loss.
  • Renal threshold for phosphate is lower in carnivores → more urinary excretion.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Faeces → correct for herbivores/ruminants, not carnivores.
  • Sweat → negligible route for P excretion in any species.
  • None → urine is the definitive answer for carnivores.

posts.post_content: Metabolic body weight is equals to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: W0.75

Metabolic body weight = W0.75, where W is live body weight in kg. This exponent (0.75) reflects the fact that basal metabolic rate scales non-linearly with body size — larger animals have lower metabolic rate per kg of body weight, but the relationship is not linear (not W1.0).

Metabolic Body Weight Concept
ParameterValue/Formula
Metabolic body weightW0.75
Basal metabolic rate (Kleiber's law)70 × W0.75 kcal/day
Maintenance energy (NRC)~77 × W0.75 kcal ME/day
Why W0.75 and Not W1.0
  • A mouse weighing 30 g has a much higher metabolic rate per gram than a 1,000 kg cow.
  • The 0.75 exponent was determined empirically by Kleiber (1932) from metabolic measurements across species.
  • Using W0.75 allows a single metabolic energy equation to apply across vastly different body sizes.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • W0.50 → square root of weight; used for surface area estimation, not metabolic weight.
  • W2.25 → has no biological basis; 2.25 is the fat-to-carbohydrate energy multiplier.
  • None → W0.75 is the universally accepted formula.

posts.post_content: Colostrum feeding in calf is done at the rate of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 10% of body weight

Colostrum feeding in calves should be done at the rate of 10% of body weight within the first 6–12 hours of birth. For a 40 kg calf, this equals 4 litres of colostrum — critical for passive immunity transfer (IgG antibodies).

Colostrum Feeding Guidelines for Calves
ParameterRecommendation
Rate of feeding10% of body weight per day
Time of first feedingWithin 1–6 hours of birth (ideally 1–2 hrs)
Duration of colostrum feedingFirst 3–4 days of life
Window for IgG absorptionFirst 24 hours (gut closure occurs at ~24–36 hrs)
Importance of Colostrum
  • Rich in Immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) — provides passive immunity to the newborn.
  • Contains Vitamin A, D, E in concentrated amounts.
  • Acts as a laxative — helps expel meconium (first faeces).
  • Contains growth factors, lysozymes, and lactoferrin for gut development.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 5% of body weight → too low; would not provide adequate immunoglobulins.
  • 15% of body weight → excessive; may cause digestive upset.
  • 20% of body weight → far too high; risk of abomasal bloat and diarrhoea.

posts.post_content: Nitrogen content of urea is ______ %.

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 46.6%

The nitrogen content of pure urea [CO(NH₂)₂] is 46.6%. This is calculated from molecular weights: N = 2 × 14 = 28; molecular weight of urea = 60; N% = 28/60 × 100 = 46.6%.

  • 1 kg urea replaces approximately 2.8 kg crude protein from natural sources.
  • Urea is fed only to ruminants ≥6 months old (functional rumen required).
  • Urea has no energy value and is deficient in all minerals.

  • 18% → nitrogen content of DAP (Diammonium Phosphate), not urea.
  • 40% → approximate N% of biuret; not urea.

posts.post_content: Balance study used to determine energy content of a feed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: C-N balance

The Carbon-Nitrogen (C-N) balance study is the balance technique used to determine energy content of feed. It involves measuring carbon intake vs carbon excreted in faeces, urine, and expired CO₂ to calculate net energy retention.

  • Outputs (faeces, urine, expired gases) are collected and analyzed for C and N.
  • Retained carbon reflects energy stored in the body as fat or protein.
  • Combined with N balance, net protein and energy utilization can be calculated.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Carbon balance alone → incomplete; the N component is also required for full energy partitioning.
  • Nitrogen balance → used for protein quality, not energy determination.
  • None → C-N balance is the specific correct answer.

posts.post_content: Nitrogen and phosphorus content of DAP fertilizer:

DAP (Diammonium Phosphate) — (NH₄)₂HPO₄ contains approximately 18% nitrogen and 46% phosphorus (as P₂O₅). It is used as an NPN source in ruminant diets and as a fertilizer. In animal nutrition, DAP provides both NPN and a significant source of available phosphorus.

  • 26% N and 46% P → N% is too high (26% is close to ammonium nitrate).

posts.post_content: Which of the following is a ketogenic amino acid?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Leucine

Leucine is the classic example of a purely ketogenic amino acid — it is degraded exclusively into Acetyl CoA and Acetoacetate, which are ketone body precursors. It cannot contribute to gluconeogenesis.

Amino Acid Classification by Metabolic Fate
CategoryExamplesProducts
Purely KetogenicLeucine (only pure one)Acetyl CoA, Acetoacetate
Glucogenic & KetogenicIsoleucine, Lysine, Phenylalanine, Tyrosine, Tryptophan, ThreonineBoth gluconeogenic and ketogenic products
Purely GlucogenicAll other amino acids (Alanine, Glutamate, etc.)Pyruvate, OAA, α-ketoglutarate

  • In starvation or uncontrolled diabetes: protein catabolism → excess Leucine → ketone body accumulation → ketosis.
  • BCAA (Branch Chain Amino Acids): Leucine, Isoleucine, Valine — metabolized in muscle, not liver.
  • Leucine also activates mTOR pathway → stimulates muscle protein synthesis.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Alanine → purely glucogenic → pyruvate → gluconeogenesis.
  • Glutamic acid → purely glucogenic → α-ketoglutarate → TCA cycle.
  • Isoleucine → both glucogenic AND ketogenic; not purely ketogenic like Leucine.

posts.post_content: Instrument used for measuring gross energy of a feed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bomb calorimeter

A Bomb calorimeter measures the Gross Energy (GE) of a feed by complete combustion. The feed sample is burned in a sealed chamber under high-pressure oxygen, and the heat released is measured. GE values: Carbohydrate = 4.15 kcal/g, Fat = 9.4 kcal/g, Protein = 5.65 kcal/g.

  • Kjeldahl apparatus → used for nitrogen/crude protein estimation, not energy.
  • Butyrometer → used to measure fat percentage in milk, not feed energy.
  • None → bomb calorimeter is the definitive instrument for GE.

posts.post_content: Maximum degradability of urea in rumen is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 100%

Urea is 100% rumen-degradable. Unlike natural proteins which have varying degradability (rumen degradable protein vs bypass protein), urea is hydrolyzed almost instantaneously by ruminal urease enzyme into NH₃ and CO₂. There is no bypass fraction for urea.

Rumen Degradability of Common Protein Sources
Protein SourceRumen Degradability (%)

Casein~90–95% (highly degradable)
Soybean meal~65–70%
Maize (corn)~40–50%
Feather meal~20–30% (high bypass)

Implications of 100% Degradability
  • Urea must be fed with sufficient rapidly fermentable carbohydrate (starch) for microbial NH₃ utilization.
  • Starch:Urea ratio of 10:1 (1 kg starch per 100 g urea) is optimal.
  • Rate of NH₃ release exceeds microbial utilization if overfed → ammonia toxicity.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 80% → applies to some high-protein meals; urea has no escape fraction.
  • 60% → typical for average feed proteins; not applicable to urea.
  • 0% → zero would mean no degradation; opposite of reality for urea.

posts.post_content: Glycolysis takes place in cytoplasm under:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both aerobic and anaerobic conditions

Glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway) occurs in the cytoplasm and can proceed under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. Under aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the mitochondria; under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate is converted to lactate (in animals) or ethanol (in yeast).

Glycolysis — Key Facts
ParameterDetail
LocationCytoplasm (cytosol)
ConditionsBoth aerobic AND anaerobic
SubstrateGlucose (or Glycogen → +1 ATP)
Net ATP yield (aerobic)38 ATP (complete oxidation)
Net ATP yield (anaerobic)2 ATP (net; 4 produced − 2 invested)
End product (aerobic)Pyruvate → enters TCA cycle
End product (anaerobic)Lactate (animals) / Ethanol (yeast)
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Aerobic only → incorrect; glycolysis was the original anaerobic pathway evolved in early life and still functions anaerobically (e.g., in exercising muscle).
  • Anaerobic only → incorrect; glycolysis also occurs under aerobic conditions as the first step of full glucose oxidation.
  • None → both conditions are correct.

posts.post_content: Method used for estimation of protein quality in ruminants as well as non-ruminants is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Nitrogen balance

Nitrogen balance is the only protein quality method applicable to BOTH ruminants and non-ruminants. It measures the difference between nitrogen (protein) intake and nitrogen excreted (in faeces + urine), reflecting net protein retention or loss in the body.

Protein Quality Evaluation Methods by Species
MethodApplicable toNotes

posts.post_title: Pathways of Urea Recycling in Ruminants
posts.post_content: The main path of urea recycling is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both a & b (via saliva AND through ruminal wall/portal blood)

Ruminants efficiently recycle endogenous urea through two pathways: (1) via saliva — the parotid and other salivary glands secrete significant amounts of urea-containing saliva into the rumen, and (2) through the ruminal wall — blood urea passes across the rumen epithelium (portal blood → rumen) by diffusion.

Urea Recycling Pathways in Ruminants
PathwayMechanismProportion of Recycling
Salivary recyclingUrea secreted in saliva → rumen~30–40% of hepatic urea
Trans-ruminal wallBlood urea → rumen epithelium → rumen~60–70% of hepatic urea
Significance of Urea Recycling
  • Allows ruminants on low-protein diets to conserve nitrogen — crucial for survival in N-deficient environments.
  • Recycled urea is hydrolyzed by rumen bacteria → NH₃ → microbial protein synthesis.
  • Total recycled urea can be 40–80% of daily urea production.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • By way of saliva only → incomplete; trans-ruminal wall passage is equally important.
  • Through ruminal wall only → incomplete; salivary recycling is also a major pathway.
  • None → both pathways are well-established and scientifically proven.

posts.post_content: Kreb's cycle takes place in mitochondria under:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Aerobic condition only

The Krebs Cycle (Citric Acid Cycle / TCA cycle) occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and requires oxygen — it is strictly an aerobic process. Without oxygen, NADH and FADH₂ produced cannot be reoxidized by the electron transport chain, so the cycle cannot continue.

Kreb's Cycle vs Glycolysis — Comparison
FeatureGlycolysisKreb's Cycle
LocationCytoplasmMitochondrial matrix
Oxygen requirementNot required (runs anaerobically too)Required (strictly aerobic)
SubstrateGlucoseAcetyl CoA
ATP yield per turn2 ATP (net)1 GTP + 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ per turn
Why Kreb's Cycle is Aerobic Only
  • NADH and FADH₂ generated by the cycle must be reoxidized by the Electron Transport Chain (ETC).
  • ETC uses O₂ as the final electron acceptor → produces H₂O.
  • Without O₂, NADH accumulates → Krebs cycle intermediates back up → cycle stops.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Anaerobic only → incorrect; the TCA cycle cannot function without oxygen.
  • Both aerobic and anaerobic → incorrect; only glycolysis can function anaerobically.
  • None → aerobic only is the correct answer.

posts.post_content: The energy of fat is how many times that of carbohydrate & protein?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2.25

Fat (lipid) contains 2.25 times more energy than carbohydrates and proteins on a gram-for-gram basis. This is used in the TDN calculation formula: TDN% = DCP% + DCF% + DNFE% + (DEE% × 2.25).

Gross Energy Values of Major Nutrients
NutrientGross Energy (kcal/g)Physiological Fuel Value (kcal/g)
Carbohydrate4.154.0
Fat9.49.0
Protein5.65 (−1.25 urinary loss)4.0
Why Fat Has Higher Energy
  • Fats have a high H:O ratio — more hydrogen atoms available for oxidation compared to carbohydrates (which are already partially oxidized).
  • Complete oxidation of fat yields more ATP per gram than carbohydrates or protein.
  • Fat provides ~9 kcal/g vs carbohydrate's ~4 kcal/g → ratio of 9/4 ≈ 2.25×.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 1.25 → the energy loss correction for protein (5.65 − 1.25 = 4.4 kcal/g for protein); not the fat:carbohydrate ratio.
  • 6.25 → the nitrogen-to-protein conversion factor (100/16 = 6.25); used in CP calculation.
  • None → 2.25 is the correct multiplier.

posts.post_content: Microbial population in rumen is controlled by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

Protozoa control the rumen microbial population because they actively prey on bacteria — engulfing and digesting bacterial cells. This predator-prey relationship determines the equilibrium of bacterial numbers in the rumen.

  • By eating bacteria, protozoa prevent excessive bacterial overgrowth
  • Defaunation (removal of protozoa) → bacterial numbers increase significantly
  • Majority of rumen protozoa are ciliate protozoa
  • Also described as "mini-ruminant" by Von Soest

  • Bacteria → the prey in this relationship; do not control the population of other microbes
  • Fungi → break down lignocellulosic material; do not control total microbial population

posts.post_content: In metabolic trial, which is/are used & collected for estimation:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both (Faeces and Urine)

In a metabolic trial, both faeces and urine are collected. This allows measurement of the complete nitrogen balance (intake − faecal N − urinary N = retained N) and energy balance of the animal.

  • BV requires both faecal and urinary nitrogen → metabolic trial, not digestibility trial

  • Urine alone → incomplete; faeces also needed to account for unabsorbed nutrients
  • Faeces alone → this is the digestibility trial, not metabolic trial
  • None → incorrect; both faeces and urine are collected in metabolic trials

  • A milk replacer is a substitute for whole milk fed to young calves
  • Goat milk is the best natural milk replacer due to similar composition and easy digestibility
  • Commercial (synthetic) milk replacers are formulated from dried skim milk, whey proteins, and fats
  • Whole milk feeding desired up to 90 days of age for proper calf growth
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Cow milk → is the baseline; we are comparing replacers to cow milk, not using cow milk itself as a replacer
  • Camel milk → high lysozyme content; used in some regions but not the standard milk replacer
  • Mare milk → used for human consumption (kumiss); not a standard calf milk replacer

posts.post_title: Major Inorganic Elements in Plants and Animals
posts.post_content: Which of the following statement is true?

_aimcq_options.text: Major inorganic elements of plants are potassium & silicon.
Major inorganic elements of animals are calcium & phosphorus.

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both a & b

Both statements are scientifically accurate: potassium and silicon are the major inorganic components of plants, while calcium and phosphorus are the major inorganic components of animals.

Major Inorganic Components
BodyMajor Inorganic ComponentsNotes
AnimalsCalcium & PhosphorusBone Ca:P ratio = 2:1; constitute ~3% of body weight
PlantsPotassium & SiliconK important in cell turgor; Si in cell walls of grasses
Mineral Composition of Animal Body
  • Total mineral content = 3% of total body weight
  • Ca: 1.33%, P: 0.74%, K: 0.19%, Na: 0.16%, S: 0.15%, Cl: 0.11%, Mg: 0.04%
  • Major cation of ECF: Na⁺; Major anion of ECF: Cl⁻
  • Major cation of ICF: K⁺; Major anion of ICF: PO₄³⁻
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Only "a" → plants have K and Si as major elements — correct, but incomplete without "b"
  • Only "b" → animals have Ca and P as major elements — correct, but incomplete without "a"
  • None → both statements are factually correct

posts.post_content: Green forages that are cut & fed in fresh condition to the animals is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both a & b

Both Green chop and Soilage refer to the same practice: fresh green forages cut and immediately fed to animals in stall/confinement (zero-grazing system).

Green Chop / Soilage — Key Facts
  • Soilage: Pasture when cut and fed green to an animal in its own stall
  • Green chop: Another term for the same practice — freshly harvested green fodder delivered to housed animals
  • Also known as zero grazing — animals do not go out to graze but feed is brought to them
  • No preservation involved; fodder is consumed fresh
Comparison of Forage Feeding Methods
MethodDescriptionPreservation?
Soilage / Green chopFresh-cut fodder fed in stallNo
SilageAnaerobic fermentationYes (months)
HaySun-dried forageYes (months–years)
HaylagePartially wilted, then ensiledYes
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Green chop alone → correct but incomplete; Soilage is the same concept
  • Soilage alone → correct but incomplete; both terms refer to the same practice
  • Haylage → partially dried and ensiled material; not fresh-cut fed fodder

posts.post_content: Milk replacer is substitute for:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Whole milk

A milk replacer is specifically a substitute for whole milk in the diet of young calves. It is used to reduce the cost of feeding whole milk while still meeting the nutritional needs of the calf.

Calf Nutrition — Stages
StageFeedPurpose
Birth – 3 daysColostrumPassive immunity transfer; immunoglobulins
Up to 90 daysWhole milkGrowth; digestive development
From 2nd weekCalf starterRumen development; early weaning
Milk replacerSubstitute for whole milkCost reduction; same nutritive value as whole milk
Calf Starter — Key Values
  • DCP: 18.5–19.5%
  • CP: 23–26%
  • TDN: 75%
  • Introduce from 2nd week of age
  • Dry feed intake → initiates rumen development → allows early weaning
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Calf starter → a solid feed introduced alongside milk; not what milk replacer replaces
  • Colostrum → first milk; cannot be replaced by a milk replacer (immunoglobulins are unique)
  • None → incorrect; whole milk is specifically what milk replacer substitutes

posts.post_content:
Match the column:

EstimationFactor used
1. Protein estimation of milk(a) 1.25
2. Protein estimation of feed stuff(b) 2.25
3. Energy estimation (TDN) of fat(c) 6.25
4. Gross energy of protein(d) 5.30
5. Protein estimation of cotton seed(e) 6.38

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1-e, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a, 5-d

These conversion factors are essential in feed analysis for calculating protein content, energy values, and gross energy from nitrogen analysis or direct measurement.

Analytical Estimation Factors — Matching
EstimationFactorDerivation / Notes
1. Protein estimation of milk(e) 6.38Milk protein contains 15.67% N → 100/15.67 ≈ 6.38
2. Protein estimation of feed stuff(c) 6.25Standard protein assumed 16% N → 100/16 = 6.25
3. Energy estimation (TDN) of fat(b) 2.25Fat has 2.25× energy value of carbohydrates (used in TDN formula)
4. Gross energy of protein(a) 1.25Urinary energy correction: protein GE (5.65) − urinary loss (1.25) = 4.4 Kcal PFV
5. Protein estimation of cotton seed(d) 5.30Cotton seed protein has higher N content → lower conversion factor
CP Calculation Rule
  • CP = N₂ content of feed × 6.25 (for most feeds)
  • CP = N₂ content of milk × 6.38 (for milk)
  • For calculating CP: assume all food protein contains 16% N
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 1-c, 2-e, 3-b, 4-d, 5-a → swaps milk protein factor (6.38) with feedstuff factor (6.25)
  • 1-e, 2-c, 3-d, 4-a, 5-b → assigns TDN fat factor (2.25) to cotton seed protein; incorrect

posts.post_content: Metabolic water comprises about ______% of total water intake of domestic animals:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 5–10%

Metabolic water is water produced inside the body during the oxidative metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. It accounts for approximately 5–10% of an animal's total water intake.

Sources of Water for Animals
SourceApproximate Contribution
Drinking water~70–80%
Water in feed~15–20%
Metabolic water~5–10%
Metabolic Water per Gram of Substrate
  • Fat: 1.07 g (highest)
  • Glucose/Sugar: 0.60 g
  • Starch: 0.56 g
  • Protein: 0.40 g (lowest)
Special Note — Camel
  • Camels store fat in their hump → fat metabolism yields high metabolic water (1.07 g/g fat) → helps survive desert conditions
  • Camel dry matter requirement: 2% of body weight (3% when working or lactating)
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 10–15% → overestimates; metabolic water is a small fraction of total water intake
  • 15–20% → too high; this is approximately the contribution of feed moisture, not metabolic water
  • None → incorrect; 5–10% is the established standard value

posts.post_title: Duration of Whole Milk Feeding for Calves
posts.post_content: For proper growth of calf, whole milk feeding is desired up to the age of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 90 days

For optimum growth and immune development, whole milk feeding is recommended up to 90 days (3 months) of age for calves. After this, the rumen is sufficiently developed for the calf to depend on solid feed.

Calf Feeding Timeline
AgeFeedReason
0–3 daysColostrum onlyPassive immunity; essential immunoglobulins
2nd week onwardsIntroduce calf starterStimulates rumen development
Up to 90 daysWhole milkEssential for growth and digestive maturation
After 90 daysSolid feed + roughageRumen functional; weaning complete
Calf Starter Composition
  • DCP: 18.5–19.5%
  • CP: 23–26%
  • TDN: 75%
  • Intake of dry feed initiates rumen development and allows early weaning
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 30 days → too early; rumen is not fully developed; calf still needs milk nutrition
  • 60 days → borderline; 90 days is the recommended standard for proper growth
  • 180 days → unnecessarily prolonged; economically wasteful and rumen is functional much earlier

posts.post_content: Calf starter contains:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 19% DCP, 25% CP & 75% TDN

A calf starter is a specially formulated concentrate feed introduced from the 2nd week of age to stimulate rumen development and support early weaning. Standard values: DCP 18.5–19.5%, CP 23–26%, TDN 75%.

Calf Starter — Nutritional Profile
NutrientValue
Digestible Crude Protein (DCP)18.5–19.5% (~19%)
Crude Protein (CP)23–26% (~25%)
Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN)75%
Introduction ageFrom 2nd week of age
Purpose of Calf Starter
  • Intake of dry feed → initiates rumen development
